Like the whole garage, the rigs, the concrete, everything would just spoil or shatter or go completely wrong if I didn't finish the sequence exactly how it was supposed to go. Voices? Like, people talking when there's nobody in the room? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. I mean, the only voices I hear are the ones I'm supposed to hear, you know? You'll be at the grocery store and hear a beep at the register and your heart rate spikes because you think you're getting a call for a cardiac arrest. That's just part of the job, the way the sounds get stuck in your head. 

But actual voices? Like someone whispering to me or telling me things when I'm alone? No. I don't have that. My problem isn't what I'm hearing, it's what they're doing. It's the paperwork, the cameras, the way they're trying to twist everything I do to make me look bad. I don't need voices in my head when I've got real people actively working against me right there in the station. They're loud enough with their actions, you know? I don't need to hear them talking when nobody's there, because I know exactly what they're saying behind my back anyway.

Well, the camera thing and the paperwork... that's been, I'd say, about two months now. Two solid months of this constant... surveillance. It started right around the time we had that bad pile-up on I-95, you know, the one where the tanker rolled? It was chaos, absolute chaos, and we were running non-stop for hours. Unwanted thoughts? No, it's not like... it's not like a thought pops into my head and says, "Hey, go do this." It's not a suggestion. It's a necessity. It's the sequence. The numbers, the bags... it's all part of the sequence. That's actually why they sent me here, you know. They didn't understand it. I was in the bay, right by the rig, and I had the airway bags out. You know the airway bags? The blue ones, with the intubation kits and the King airways? I had them out, and I was moving them into the pattern. The pattern I knew was right. Because if they aren't in the right pattern, the sequence is broken, and if the sequence is broken, the whole bay goes bad. 

And the numbers, the dispatch numbers... I have to repeat them out loud. It's not an unwanted thought, it's just what has to happen. You repeat the numbers to lock the sequence in place. It's like... it's like setting the parking brake on the rig. You don't just think about setting it, you actually pull the lever so the truck doesn't roll away. Repeating the numbers out loud is pulling the lever. So I was doing that, setting the bags in the pattern, saying the numbers, and my lieutenant—Lieutenant Harris, who, by the way, is definitely one of the ones changing my paperwork—he comes over and tells me to stop. He's yelling at me to step away from the bags. 

But I couldn't step away. I wouldn't do it. I couldn't just stop in the middle of the sequence. If I stopped, the whole bay would go bad. Everything would just... unravel. The calls would go wrong, the rig wouldn't start, the paperwork would get even more twisted up. I had to finish it. So I kept going, putting the bags in the right spots, saying the numbers, and he's getting louder, telling me I'm off the truck, telling me I need a psych eval. That's how I ended up sitting here talking to you. Because they couldn't see that I was actually keeping things from going bad. They just saw me arranging the bags and repeating the numbers and decided I was the problem. But it wasn't an unwanted thought making me do it. It was the only way to keep the sequence intact.

It’s like, the angles have to align perfectly or it doesn't work. And I was... I guess I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I was doing it. The call numbers from the radio, you know? Just saying them over and over, because the numbers anchor the pattern. They lock it in. \n\nMy lieutenant came out and he told me to stop. He was getting loud, telling me to step away from the bags and go up to the office, but I couldn't. I wouldn't step away. He didn't understand that if I stopped, if I broke that sequence before it was finished... it felt like the whole bay would go bad. Like the whole garage, the rigs, the concrete, everything would just spoil or shatter or go completely wrong if I didn't finish the sequence exactly how it was supposed to go. I couldn't let that happen. So I wouldn't stop, and... well, they made me come here.\n\nDoctor: When you were arranging the airway bags, did part of you realize that the idea that everything would spoil or shatter if you stopped might not actually be true?\n\nPatient: No, no, you’re not hearing me. It’s not about whether it’s true or not, it *is* true. I felt it. It’s like a physical weight in the air, you know? Like when the barometric pressure drops before a massive storm and you can feel it in your joints, in your teeth even. That’s what it was like. If I stopped, the whole structure of the place was going to collapse in on itself, just spoil right there on the concrete. And see, the thing is, I had to make sure the bags were right because... well, because I know they’re already trying to build a case against me. \n\nIt’s the injury review people, and some of the supervisors, too. They’re watching me. They’ve got the station cameras—the ones in the bay, the ones by the lockers, even the one near the dispatch desk that’s supposed to be broken, I know it’s not broken. They’re watching every move I make, tracking my sequences, and then they go into the system and they change my triage notes. My paperwork. I’ll write down a perfectly good assessment, standard protocol, ABCs, everything by the book, and then later I’ll look and it’s been altered. They change the vitals I recorded, they change the interventions, just to make it look like I’m unsafe. Like I don’t know what I’m doing. And when I try to bring it up, when I say, \"Hey, this isn't what I wrote, someone’s been in my files,\" they just look at me with these blank faces and tell me it’s just routine paperwork. \"Oh, it’s just a system glitch,\" or \"Oh, it’s just routine auditing.\" Routine! It’s not routine. They’re actively rewriting my reality on paper to make me look incompetent, which is exactly why I couldn't let them interrupt me with the bags. If I let them break the pattern, they win. They get exactly what they want.\n\nDoctor: Have you been needing much less sleep than usual lately and still feeling full of energy?\n\nPatient: No, no, sleep isn't... I mean, I'm sleeping. It's not like I'm staying up for days on end bouncing off the walls or anything like that. I'm getting my rest. Well, as much rest as anyone can get when they work the shifts I do, right? You're on a 24-hour rotation, you're sleeping in the bunk room with one ear open anyway, waiting for the tones to drop. It's a different kind of sleep. You're never really fully out because the radio is always right there on your hip or on the nightstand, and you have to be ready to jump into your boots and be in the rig in under two minutes. \n\nBut lately, even when I'm off shift, even when I'm home in my own bed... I mean, I'm sleeping, but it's not like I wake up feeling like I could run a marathon. I'm tired. I'm actually really, really tired. It's exhausting having to keep track of everything, you know? Watching the cameras, checking my paperwork, making sure the sequences are right... it takes a lot out of you. It's not like I have some kind of endless supply of energy. I wish I did. Honestly, if I had more energy, maybe I could catch them in the act of changing my triage notes. But no, I'm sleeping my usual amount, maybe even a little more when I can, but it doesn't seem to make a dent in how heavy everything feels. It's just a constant, grinding kind of exhaustion, not this full-of-energy thing you're talking about. I'm just... I'm just trying to keep my head above water with all of this going on.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever hear voices when no one is there?\n\nPatient: Voices? Like, people talking when there's nobody in the room? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. I mean, the only voices I hear are the ones I'm supposed to hear, you know? The dispatchers over the radio, my partner complaining about the suspension on the rig, the patients when we're trying to get a history out of them. That's it. It's not like I'm sitting in an empty room having a conversation with a ghost or something. \n\nI mean, sure, it gets noisy. It gets really loud, actually. But it's a different kind of loud. It's the hum of the fluorescent lights in the bay, which, by the way, they really need to change the ballasts on those things because they have this high-pitched whine that just burrows right into your skull if you stand under them too long. And the tones... you hear the tones in your sleep sometimes, the drop before a call comes in. Any EMT will tell you that. You'll be at the grocery store and hear a beep at the register and your heart rate spikes because you think you're getting a call for a cardiac arrest. That's just part of the job, the way the sounds get stuck in your head. \n\nBut actual voices? Like someone whispering to me or telling me things when I'm alone? No. I don't have that. I don't need voices in my head when I've got real people actively working against me right there in the station. They're loud enough with their actions, you know? I don't need to hear them talking when nobody's there, because I know exactly what they're saying behind my back anyway.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been dealing with people watching you and changing your paperwork?\n\nPatient: Well, the camera thing and the paperwork... that's been, I'd say, about two months now. Two solid months of this constant... surveillance. It started right around the time we had that bad pile-up on I-95, you know, the one where the tanker rolled? It was chaos, absolute chaos, and we were running non-stop for hours. And right after that, I started noticing the little things. At first, I thought maybe I was just misremembering my own notes because I was so exhausted from that shift, but then it kept happening. \n\nI'd look at my tablet, and a blood pressure reading I knew for a fact I typed in as 120 over 80 would suddenly say 140 over 90. And the cameras, I started noticing the red lights on them staying on longer, tracking me when I walked across the bay to check the rig's oil. I even tested it once, I took two steps to the left and stopped, and the lens physically panned to follow me. \n\nSo yeah, two months of this. Two months of having to double, triple check every single keystroke, every single form, making sure I have a mental backup of every intervention I perform. It's like... it's like setting the parking brake on the rig. You don't just think about setting it, you actually pull the lever so the truck doesn't roll away. Repeating the numbers out loud is pulling the lever. So I was doing that, setting the bags in the pattern, saying the numbers, and my lieutenant—Lieutenant Harris, who, by the way, is definitely one of the ones changing my paperwork—he comes over and tells me to stop. He's yelling at me to step away from the bags. \n\nBut I couldn't step away. I wouldn't do it. I couldn't just stop in the middle of the sequence. If I stopped, the whole bay would go bad. Everything would just... unravel. The calls would go wrong, the rig wouldn't start, the paperwork would get even more twisted up. I had to finish it. Talking less or feeling flat? I mean... yeah, I guess you could say that. But it's more than just feeling flat. It's like... it's like someone pulled the plug on the whole system, you know?
